passages.text: The role of right ventricular systolic pressure and ARISCAT score in perioperative pulmonary risk assessment
Background

Postoperative Pulmonary Complications (PPC) are a significant source of increased morbidity and mortality after surgical procedures. Measures to enhance 30-day PPC risk stratification are an area of significant clinical interest, and integrating common preoperative investigations, such as echocardiography, may enhance quantitative risk prediction when combined with clinical score-based systems, particularly for high-risk populations. The authors hypothesized that Right Ventricular Systolic Pressure (RVSP) would significantly enhance the predictive capabilities of the Assess Respiratory Risk in Surgical Patients in Catalonia (ARISCAT) score in the prediction of 30-day PPC in a Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) study cohort.
Methods

277 patients with the diagnosis of PH, ARISCAT score, and echocardiography-derived RVSP within 12-months of surgical procedure were analyzed. The primary endpoint was the 59-variable 30-day Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality PPC composite. Secondary endpoints included sub composites of Pneumonia (PNA), Respiratory Failure (RF), Pulmonary Aspiration (ASP) and thromboembolic Phenomenon (PE). Adjusted multivariable logistic regression models followed by Receiver Operating Characteristic Curves (ROC) and Area Under the Curve (AUC) analysis were employed to assess the prediction of 30-day PPC.
Results

Mean RVSP was 52.1 mmHg (+-17.4). Overall PPC incidence was 29.9%, with RF (19.5%), PNA (12.3%), ASP (5.4%), and PE (3.6%) composites. Logistic regression showed no significant association between RVSP and PPC (Odds Ratio [OR = 1.01], p = 0.307). The ARISCAT score was associated with 30-day PPC risk (OR = 1.02, p = 0.037). Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis revealed an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.555 for RVSP alone, 0.575 for the ARISCAT score, and 0.591 for the combination of RVSP+ARISCAT for the primary endpoint.
Conclusion

RVSP demonstrated limited efficacy as a standalone predictor of 30-day PPC in patients with PH. Although integrating RVSP with ARISCAT scoring yielded marginal improvements in predictive accuracy, neither metric, independently or in combination, achieved adequate clinical significance for reliable risk stratification. These findings highlight a critical gap in the current preoperative risk assessment for PH-specific predictive tools. Future research should focus on alternative measures that better capture vulnerability to the hemodynamic complexities underscoring PPC in this high-risk population.
Introduction

Postoperative Pulmonary Complications (PPC) are a significant source of increased morbidity and mortality after surgical procedures. Measures to enhance 30-day PPC risk stratification are an area of significant clinical interest, and integrating common preoperative investigations, such as echocardiography, may enhance quantitative risk prediction when combined with clinical score-based systems, particularly for high-risk populations. Right Ventricular Systolic Pressure (RVSP) is commonly estimated during preoperative Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE) using the modified Bernoulli equation [RVSP (mmHg) = 4TRV2 + RAP, where TRV, Tricuspid Regurgitation Velocity (m/sec) and RAP, Right Atrial Pressure (mmHg)]. Right ventricular systolic pressure is a correlate for right ventricular afterload, and the American College of Cardiology recommends further evaluation of patients with dyspnea and RVSP > 40 mmHg to assess for the presence of Pulmonary Hypertension (PH). In perioperative settings, PH is associated with significant cardiopulmonary morbidity and mortality. Given the frequency, economic impact, and increased morbidity of PPC, improving PPC risk prediction is vital for developing preventive perioperative strategies.

RVSP alone and in combination with the Assess Respiratory Risk in Surgical Patients in Catalonia (ARISCAT) score, a validated PPC risk scoring system for general populations, were evaluated to determine if quantitative echocardiographic measures could enhance PPC risk prediction. ARISCAT incorporates factors such as age, preoperative arterial oxyhemoglobin saturation, recent respiratory infection, anemia, surgical site, procedure duration, and urgency to predict in-hospital PPC risk. While ARISCAT is used to predict in-hospital PPC, recent reports have suggested that its predictive capabilities extend to 30-day PPC. Acknowledging the risk of 30-day PPC is critically important, as recent reports indicate that the trend toward shorter postoperative length of stays has led to an increase in post-discharge infections and other complications. The primary objective of this study was to assess whether increasing RVSP alone, or in tandem with ARISCAT predicts 30-day PPC risk in a PH population. The authors hypothesized that Right Ventricular Systolic Pressure (RVSP) would significantly enhance the predictive capabilities of the Assess Respiratory Risk in Surgical Patients in Catalonia (ARISCAT) score in the prediction of 30-day PPC in a Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) study cohort.
Methods
Study population
CONSORT flow diagram of patient study inclusion.
Figure 1

This retrospective cohort study was approved by the Yale University Institutional Review Board (IRB#2000032516) with a waiver of informed consent. 1,747 patients with International Classification of Disease version 10 (ICD-10) codes for PH (I27.0, I27.2) who underwent elective inpatient abdominal surgery or gastrointestinal endoscopic procedures at Yale New Haven Hospital between 2013 and 2020 were analyzed. Patients aged < 18 or > 90 years, classified as American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification System (ASA-PS) V or VI, and procedures without general anesthesia were excluded. To avoid duplicates in patients with multiple surgical encounters, only the most recent procedure was analyzed. Among 876 eligible patients, 277 with preoperative ARISCAT scores and echocardiographic RVSP within 12-months of surgery were analyzed (Fig. 1).
Outcomes

Baseline characteristics included age, Body Mass Index (BMI), Elixhauser comorbidities, and procedure severity, which was classified using the Surgical Outcome Risk Tool (SORT) v2. The outcomes included 30-day PPC and 30-day mortality. ARISCAT scores were individually tabulated, and PPC was defined using the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) PPC composite criteria (Supplementary Table 1). PPC subcategories included Respiratory Failure (RF), Pneumonia (PNA), Aspiration (ASP), and Thromboembolic Phenomena (PE).
Statistical analysis

Logistic regression analysis was performed to evaluate RVSP and ARISCAT as predictors of PPC and subcategories. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to calculate the Area Under the Curve (AUC) for RVSP, ARISCAT, and RVSP+ARISCAT, with and without covariate adjustments using propensity score weighting for age, BMI, Elixhauser comorbidities, and procedure severity. PH patients were further classified into RVSP >= 40 mmHg and RVSP < 40 mmHg groups and reanalyzed using similar methods. Only subjects with complete information were included in the analysis.
Results
Baseline characteristics
Baseline characteristics of the studied cohort categorized by presence of right ventricular systolic pressure >= 40 mmHg or < 40 mmHg.

The final cohort included 277 patients (59.9% female) with a mean age of 66.4 years (+-14.5), a mean BMI of 29.4 (+-8.9), and a median Elixhauser comorbidity count of 7 (Interquartile Range [IQR = 5-8]). Procedural severity was classified as intermediate (62.5%), major (19.9%), and Xmajor/complex (17.7%). The median surgery duration was 92.5 minutes (IQR = 51-170]. Mean RVSP was 52.1 mmHg (+-17.4). Overall, the 30-day PPC incidence was 29.9% (n = 83), and 30-day mortality rate was 3.9% (n = 11). Patients with and without PPC did not differ significantly different with respect to any of the aforementioned baseline characteristics (p > 0.05) (Table 1).
Primary endpoint
Adjusted logistic regression analysis showed no association between RVSP and PPC (Odds Ratio (OR) = 1.01, 95% Confidence Interval (95% CI) 0.99-1.02, p = 0.307).
Secondary endpoints

After adjustment, the ARISCAT score was associated with 30-day PPC (ORadj = 1.02, 95% CI 1.00-1.03, p = 0.037). The ARISCAT score was associated with RF (ORadj = 1.02, 95% CI 1.00-1.04, p = 0.020) but not with PNA (ORadj = 1.01, 95% CI 0.99-1.03, p = 0.348), ASP (OR = 1.0, 95% CI 0.97-1.03, p = 0.981), or PE (OR = 1.01, 95% CI 0.97-1.05, p = 0.594). RVSP was not associated with any of the sub composites, including RF (OR = 1.01, 95% CI 0.99-1.03, p = 0.179), PNA (OR = 1.00, 95% CI0.97-1.02, p = 0.710), ASP (OR = 0.99, 95% CI 0.96-1.02, p = 0.523), or PE (OR = 1.02, 95% CI 0.99-1.05, p = 0.212).

Although the combination was highly predictive for 30-day thromboembolic events, it requires further validation in a larger cohort. PPC, Postoperative Pulmonary Complications; RVSP, Right Ventricular Systolic Pressure by echocardiography; ARISCAT, the Assess Respiratory Risk in Surgical Patients in Catalonia risk index.
Figure 2

The AUC values were 0.555 for RVSP alone, 0.575 for ARISCAT, and 0.658 for the hybridized RVSP and ARISCAT (Supplementary Table 2). The results remained consistent before and after covariate adjustment. In the subgroup analysis, patients with RVSP >= 40 mmHg (n = 210) and RVSP < 40 mmHg (n = 67) did not show a significant difference in PPC (32% vs. 24%, p = 0.273), RF (21% vs. 15%, p = 0.339), PNA (13% vs. 10%, p = 0.729), ASP (5.3% vs. 6.0%, p = 1), PE (3.9% vs. 3.0%, p = 1), or 30-day mortality (4.1% vs. 3.5%, p = 1.0). Similarly, few differences were observed when categorized by RHC (Supplementary Table 3). Hybridized ARISCAT+RVSP consistently outperformed for patients with RVSP < 40, with the exception of RF (Fig. 2).
Discussion

In summary, RVSP alone was not associated with PPC risk. However, the ARISCAT score, originally validated for general surgical populations and in-hospital pulmonary complications, showed a significant association with 30-day PPC in PH patients. While RVSP enhanced ARISCAT's predictive power for specific subcategories (RF, PNA, and PE), the overall clinical relevance of this improvement was minimal.

Although elevated RVSP remains an important prognostic factor for PH, interstitial lung disease as well as a marker for low functional capacity by the Duke Activity Status Index, this study's findings revealed that abnormal RVSP was not a reliable marker for 30-day PPC in PH populations. Interestingly, RVSP provided incremental enhancement of ARISCAT in hybrid classification plots, suggesting improved prediction of 30-day PPC, PNA, and ASP but not RF in patients with RVSP < 40 mmHg. RVSP likely provides a snapshot of overall right heart health, whereas surgical stress requires more dynamic, individualized measures to predict vulnerability to respiratory insufficiency and failure. Static RVSP values may overlook the pulsatile nature of right ventricular work and its complex interactions with postoperative hemodynamic shifts, such as fluid overload, which underlies a large number of postoperative respiratory insufficiency/failure events. Alternative measures, such as pulmonary vascular impedance, warrant investigation as more sensitive markers for PPC vulnerability in PH populations. Recent publications have shown the predictive strength of measured pulmonary capacitance for prognosis quantification in PH and CHF, suggesting that it may be a compelling investigational target for PPC risk prediction. Interestingly, patients with RHC within 24-months of procedure were younger, had higher Elixhauser scores, but lower preoperative ARISCAT scores (p < 0.001). Although the significance is unclear, it suggests that these patients were better optimized prior to surgical procedures, given that there were no significant differences in PPC outcomes.

While higher ARISCAT score was associated with 30-day PPC, its clinical predictive strength remained limited for the robust AHRQ-PPC composite. The original ARISCAT focused on in-hospital PPC events. In contrast, the AHRQ-PPC composite includes important diagnoses such as pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, enhanced coding for respiratory failure/insufficiency, and extends PPC capture from procedure date through thirty days. The AHRQ-PPC composite offers broader complication capture, which is particularly important given the contemporary trend of shorter LOS. Despite this, sub composite analysis incorporating RVSP showed only modest improvement, failing to reach clinically significant levels (AUC > 0.8) despite all iterations showing modest improvement. Classification plots including hybridized ARISCAT+RVSP did demonstrate variable predictive power, when divided by RVSP thresholds. RVSP < 40 patients demonstrated improved PPC risk prediction using the hybridized ARISCAT+RVSP, while RVSP >= 40 prediction was diminished. The findings suggest that while current risk assessment tools provide valuable insights, there remains a significant opportunity to develop more robust, PH-specific predictive models that account for the complex pathophysiology of this patient population.
Limitations

The study's findings have several factors that limit generalizability, including (1) Selection bias due to exclusion of patients with missing data, (2) Echocardiographic RVSP measurement variability, including its dependence on adequate tricuspid regurgitation and technical proficiency, and (3) Unmeasured confounding factors. The study population comprised of patients with ICD-10 coding of PH, highlighting the potential for inaccurate diagnosis. Out of 277 patients in this study, 93 underwent RHC within 24 months of surgery, and 87 of those 93 patients had mPAP > 20 mmHg. This implied a partial but reasonable positive predictive value for ICD-10 coding; however, it still limits the generalizability of the findings.
Conclusion

RVSP demonstrated limited efficacy as a standalone predictor of 30-day PPC in patients with PH. Although integrating RVSP with ARISCAT scoring yielded marginal improvements in predictive accuracy, neither metric, independently or in combination, achieved adequate clinical significance for reliable risk stratification. These findings highlight a critical gap in the current preoperative risk assessment for PH-specific predictive tools. Future research should focus on alternative measures that better capture vulnerability to the hemodynamic complexities underscoring PPC in this high-risk population.

passages.text: In silico evaluation of N-aryl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines as potential inhibitors of T. cruzi GP63 zinc-metalloprotease by docking and molecular dynamics simulations

Based on the in vitro trypanocidal efficacy of previously synthesized N-aryl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines (Phen1-20) (aryl = R-phenyl, 1- or 2-naphthyl), we explored the potential interactions of these derivatives as ligands of our comparative model of T. cruzi GP63 (TcGP63). This surface metalloprotease plays a crucial role in parasite adhesion to host cells and aids in cell invasion during T. cruzi infection in Chagas disease. Ligand-protein consensus docking simulations using four GOLD scoring functions revealed that N-(R-phenyl) derivatives (R = CH3, OCH3, CF3, CN, NO2, F, Cl, and Br) presented poses with higher fitness scores than the N-naphthyl ones, with the six para-substituted derivatives (Phen4, p-CH3; Phen7, p-OCH3; Phen10, p-CN; Phen14, p-F; Phen17, p-Cl; and Phen18, p-Br) being more favorable than the ortho or meta ones. Subsequent aqueous molecular dynamics simulation (GROMACS package, CHARMM36 force field, and TIP3P water model) of the ligand-protein complexes for these six top-ranking compounds showed persistent interactions within the TcGP63 active site, primarily through coordination with Zn(II)-cofactor, and H-bonding with catalytic Glu221 and zinc-binding His224. RMSD and RMSF analyses confirmed the stability of these interactions, particularly for compounds with electron-withdrawing groups by inductive effect as R-substituents, such as p-OCH3 (Phen7) and p-CN (Phen10). Binding free energy calculations by the linear interaction energy (LIE) approach corroborated the favorable interactions observed in simulations, highlighting Phen7 and Phen10 as the most promising candidates. This study underscores the potential of N-phenyl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines as putative inhibitors targeting the T. cruzi GP63 enzyme.

Introduction

Among the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the United Nations 2030 Agenda, target 3.3 of SDG 3 - Good health and well-being - includes, by 2030, end the epidemics of neglected diseases, also known as neglected tropical diseases (NTDs). More than one billion people worldwide are affected by NTDs, including Chagas disease (CD) (or American trypanosomiasis), a parasitic infection endemic to 21 countries in Latin America, affecting about 6-7 million people.

Trypanosoma cruzi, a protozoan parasite, is the etiological agent of CD, and its biological cycle is complex and heterogeneous, involving insect vectors from the Reduviidae family and mammalian hosts. The life cycle consists of an insect stage (vector), where the triatomine bug, also known as the "kissing bug", becomes infected by feeding on the blood of an infected host. The parasite multiplies in the bug's gut and is excreted in its feces. In the human stage (mammalian host), when the bug bites a human, it often defecates near the bite wound. The T. cruzi parasites enter the host's body through the wound or mucous membranes. The parasites then invade various cells, multiply, and transform into different life stages.

In addition to vector-human transmission, there are other possible means, such as congenital transmission from an infected mother to her baby during pregnancy or childbirth, blood transfusion, or organ transplantation from infected donors. Moreover, the transmission through the ingestion of food and drinks contaminated with the insect's feces has been reported in several countries, mainly in Latin America, such as Brazil, Colombia, and Argentina.

Chagas disease has two phases: acute and chronic. The acute phase occurs shortly after infection and may be mild or asymptomatic. Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, body aches, rash, and swelling at the infection site. The acute phase lasts for a few weeks or months. The chronic phase can occur decades after the initial infection. It may lead to severe complications such as cardiomyopathy, digestive tract issues, and neurological disorders. Chronic CD can be life-threatening if untreated.

Studying this pathogen presents challenges due to its unique biology, evolutionary stages, adaptability to various environments, and the distinct phenotypes observed among different strains. The disease has a complicated pathophysiology, characterized by an acute phase that can transition into a chronic phase, with the parasite persisting in the host for many years.

Despite being discovered over a century ago, the factors that determine the clinical progression of CD still need to be clarified. Both host factors, such as the immune system and parasite factors, including strain variations and routes of infection, play roles in the disease's pathophysiology, which often involves myocardial and intestinal complications in its chronic phase. However, there is still much to learn about what influences the parasite's persistence and its preference for specific tissues within the host. Furthermore, the treatment of CD patients is still based only on two trypanocide nitro compounds acting as prodrugs, namely, benznidazole and nifurtimox, which are highly toxic and are used to treat the infection, especially in the acute phase. Treatment is less effective in the chronic phase but can slow disease progression.

The biological complexity of the parasite, mainly due to its heteroxenic life cycle, genetic variability, and environmental adaptation, makes it necessary to develop new drugs to combat CD. Studies also indicate that T. cruzi can develop resistance to existing treatments, such as benznidazole and nifurtimox, requiring new compounds with different mechanisms of action to prevent cross-resistance.

One potential approach involves studying molecular targets of the pathogen that may affect infection progression and parasite survival. One of the crucial enzymes of the T. cruzi parasite in the interaction with host cells is the surface glycoprotein 63 (TcGP63) (i.e., leishmanolysin-like peptidase or peptidase family M8), a zinc metalloprotein with a proteolytic activity based on a zinc-binding HEXXH motif, and a more C-terminal histidine residue that is the third ligand of zinc, playing an essential role in parasite adhesion to host cells and aids in cell invasion during T. cruzi infection. It was demonstrated that T. cruzi has a family of GP63 genes composed of multiple groups (I-IV), two of them are highly expressed (TcGP63-I and TcGP63-II), and that the TcGP63-I metalloprotease is sensitive toward the metal-chelating 1,10-phenanthroline, as was described for the homologous Leishmania GP63 (i.e., leishmanolysin) metalloenzyme.

Additionally, GP63 can break down components of the host's immune system, allowing the parasite to evade immune responses. It also interferes with cell signaling and apoptosis, influencing the inflammatory response and promoting parasite survival. By degrading host proteins, GP63 assists the parasite in avoiding detection and destruction by the immune system and in the penetration, dissemination, and spread of infection within various host tissues. GP63 inhibitors can be developed to block the function of this protease and thus reduce the parasite's ability to infect and damage host tissues. In this way, GP63 is considered a potential therapeutic target due to its critical role in the survival and pathogenicity of T. cruzi.

Research into NTDs, such as Chagas disease, often receives less funding and attention than other more prevalent diseases. Therefore, technologies such as in silico studies based on molecular docking and dynamics simulations focus on attractive drug targets such as GP63. The scientific community currently employs these methods to study new anti-Chagas agents, evaluate molecular inhibition mechanisms, explore binding sites, and design selective inhibitors targeting a range of proteins and enzymes of the parasite, hurrying the identification of compounds and consequently are an alternative for the discovery of new drugs with different mechanisms of antiparasitic action.

In our previous studies, 1,10-phenanthroline and a series of N-aryl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines (aryl = phenyl and naphthyl) were reported due to their effective trypanocidal activity against amastigote (IC50 from 0.5 to 3 microM), epimastigote (IC50 from 0.5 to at least 10 microM), and trypomastigote (and LD50 from 1 to10 microM) forms of T. cruzi. At the same time, they were non-toxic to mammalian cells (CC50 >= 20 microM). Hence, this current study aimed to verify whether these compounds exhibiting anti-trypanosomal activity could serve as potential inhibitors of the T. cruzi GP63 metalloenzyme, since 1,10-phenanthroline itself is a known chelating ligand for transition metal ions, such as zinc, and an inhibitor of other zinc-dependent metalloenzymes. Therefore, we conducted a structure-based molecular modeling investigation of these N-aryl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines by consensus ligand-protein molecular docking (GOLD software) and aqueous molecular dynamics simulations (GROMACS package, CHARMM36 force field, and TIP3P water model), including binding free energy calculations by the linear interaction energy (LIE) end-point method, to elucidate their potential binding interaction with the TcGP63 metalloenzyme as a target that justifies the in vitro trypanocidal activity observed for these compounds.
Results and discussion
Binding mode analysis by molecular docking simulations

Based on the trypanocidal activity of N-aryl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines (Phen1-20) (aryl = R-phenyl, 1- or 2-naphthyl) previously synthesized and tested by our group, we decided to investigate by molecular docking simulations the potential interactions of these compounds with our 3D comparative model of T. cruzi GP63 (TcGP63) (available in the ModelArchive repository, see "Materials and methods" Section), which is based on the experimental X-ray structure of Leishmania major GP63.

The consensus docking simulation of the 20 compounds into the active site of the TcGP63 model was conducted using the four scoring functions of the GOLD program, namely GS (GoldScore), PLP (ChemPLP, piecewise linear potential), CS (ChemScore), and ASP (Astex statistical potential), resulting in ligand-protein poses and their respective fitness score (FS) values (Table 1). The consensus docking based on scoring, previously described for the TcGP63 enzyme, is crucial to overcome the absence of a co-crystallized ligand, thereby providing more reliable predictions of ligand binding modes to the target protein.

passages.text: We observed that all N-(R-phenyl) derivatives (Phen1-18) exhibited higher FS values than the two N-naphthyl compounds (Phen19-20) considering all scoring functions. Indeed, by examining the cross-correlation matrix of FS values for all scoring functions, we found a high degree of correlation (r >= 0.980), most notable between the following pairs: CS vs. ASP (0.999) and GS vs. PLP (r = 0.999) (Table S1). Furthermore, analyzing the ortho, meta, or para position of the R-substituents at the N-(R-phenyl) ring showed that the para-position was more favorable than the ortho- or meta-positions for all scoring functions (Table 1).

We could rank the compounds using a single metric using the scaled fitness scores (SFS) values for each scoring function and their total sum that combines all SFS values (Table S2). Out of the 20 derivatives evaluated (Table S2), the results showed scaled total sum values ranging from 0 to 4.01 when considering the FS of the four scoring functions. The top six total sum scores were for the para-substituted N-(R-phenyl) compounds with R = p-OCH3 (Phen7, total sum = 4.01), p-CN (Phen10, total sum = 3.97), p-F (Phen14, total sum = 3.82), p-CH3 (Phen4, total sum = 3.81), p-Cl (Phen17, total sum = 3.77), and p-Br (Phen18, total sum = 3.71). This led us to establish selection criteria for further investigating these six selected compounds that demonstrated similar values (Table S2).

These top six compounds were assessed for their interactions with the TcGP63 target based on the consensus pose of RMSD analysis among the four score functions and for all complexes resulting from molecular docking, the lowest RMSD value was obtained between the CS vs. ASP functions score ranging from 0.02 to 0.08 A (Table S3).

It is important to note that the active site of the TcGP63 enzyme (UniProtKB: Q9NG31_TRYCR) consists of a nucleophilic glutamic acid residue (catalytic Glu221) and that the Zn(II) cofactor is coordinated by three histidine residues including His220 and His224 from the zinc-binding HEXXH motif, and His289 from the C-terminal region.

The ligand-protein docking poses for the top six compounds (Phen4, Phen7, Phen10, Phen14, Phen17, and Phen18) revealed that they all show the same binding mode, located in the TcGP63 active site (Fig. 1). As expected, the two nitrogen atoms, N(1) and N(10), of the bidentate 1,10-phenanthroline nucleus, common to all compounds, act as a fourth Zn(II) ligand. Therefore, the Zn(II) center displays a distorted tetrahedral geometry, coordinating through one N-donor atom from each of the three monodentate zinc-binding histidine residues (His220, His224, and His289) and two N-donor atoms of one bidentate 1,10-phenanthroline nucleus ligand. The 2-amino group (NH, H-bond donor), a linker between the R-substituted phenyl and 1,10-phenanthroline rings, was also crucial for interacting with the TcGP63 enzyme, forming a hydrogen bond with the main chain carbonyl group (C = O, H-bond acceptor) of the Gly284 residue in all cases (Fig. 1).

Notably, it was observed for all six compounds that the phenyl ring adopts a conformation almost completely perpendicular to the plane of the 1,10-phenanthroline ring, allowing the establishment of a parallel pi-pi stacking interaction between the N-phenyl ring of the ligands and imidazole ring of the zinc-binding His224 residue (Fig. 1). Except for compounds Phen10 (p-CN, Fig. 1C) and Phen14 (p-F, Fig. 1D), which exhibited the aforementioned pi-pi stacking interaction, the other compounds (Phen4, p-CH3; Phen7, p-OCH3; Phen17, p-Cl; and Phen18, p-Br; Fig. 1A-B and E-F) additionally showed pi-alkyl type interactions between the R-substituents (CH3, OCH3, Cl, and Br) and the His224 imidazole ring.

Molecular dynamics simulations

With the aim of better understanding how the top six best-ranking compounds (Phen4, p-CH3; Phen7, p-OCH3; Phen10, p-CN; Phen14, p-F; Phen17, p-Cl; and Phen18, p-Br) from the previous docking analysis interacted with the molecular target, we carried out 200 ns of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with the GROMACS package and CHARMM36 force field of these six N-phenyl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines as ligands of the TcGP63 model to observe the dynamic behavior of the interaction modes in an aqueous (TIP3P) system.

The analysis of the protein alpha-carbon (alpha-carbon or Calpha) atoms root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) revealed a standard behavior for all ligand-protein complexes throughout the 200 ns of simulation (Fig. 2A-F). Phen18 (4.19 +- 0.63 A), Phen7 (4.31 +- 0.70 A), Phen10 (4.37 +- 0.75 A), Phen14 (4.57 +- 1.18 A), and Phen17 (4.93 +- 0.83 A) showed an average RMSD variation ranging from 4.19 A to 4.93 A, whereas Phen4 (5.94 +- 1.29 A) presented the highest mean Calpha-RMSD. This behavior can be attributed to conformational changes occurring up to 50 ns, followed by a return to a conformation close to the initial state by the end of the simulation. Moreover, the ligand-enzyme complexes Calpha-RMSD mean and standard deviation values are similar to those observed for the holoenzyme form (5.82 +- 0.90 A) (Fig. S1). The stability of the complexes can be evaluated by verifying that the standard deviation of the Calpha-RMSD remains below 2 A.

Protein Calpha-RMSD graph of the Trypanosoma cruzi GP63 metalloenzyme model in complex with Phen4 (A), Phen7 (B), Phen10 (C), Phen14 (D), Phen17 (E), and Phen18 (F), during 200 ns of aqueous molecular dynamics simulations (GROMACS package, CHARMM36 force field, and TIP3P water model).

The RMSD analysis between the centers of mass of the protein's Calpha atoms and the ligand showed that Phen7 (p-OCH3), Phen10 (p-CN), Phen14 (p-F), and Phen17 (p-Cl) remained at an average distance ranging from 3.80 A to 5.73 A, with a standard deviation below 1 A, demonstrating the stability of these compounds throughout the simulation (Fig. S2). In contrast, Phen4 (p-CH3) and Phen18 (p-Br) tended to leave the active site, with Phen4 exiting more gradually, while Phen18 underwent an abrupt distancing after 130 ns of simulation (Fig. S2).

Next, we evaluated the distance between the nitrogen atom in the 1,10-phenanthroline ring and the zinc ion to assess the stability of the Zn-N coordination bond (Fig. 3A, B). Our MD simulations demonstrated notable proximity between the metal and the nitrogen atoms of compounds Phen7 (p-OCH3), Phen10 (p-CN), Phen14 (p-F), and Phen17 (p-Cl) (Fig. 3A). In general, compounds containing electron-withdrawing groups by inductive effect as R-substituents, such as p-OCH3, p-CN, p-F, and p-Cl, remained in closer proximity when coordinated with Zn(II), exhibiting average distance values of 2.21 +- 0.1 A (Phen7), 2.19 +- 0.1 A (Phen10), 2.18 +- 0.1 A (Phen14), and 2.57 +- 0.02 A (Phen17), which were stable throughout the simulation (Fig. 3A).

These average values are consistent with those reported in the literature for coordinating Zn(II) and nitrogen atoms, such as in two experimental crystal structures of horse liver alcohol dehydrogenase, a zinc-metallodehydrogenase, in complex with bidentate nitrogen chelating agents, namely 1,10-phenanthroline (PDB ID: 5VJ5; Zn-N distances of 2.309 A and 2.404 A) and 2,2'-bipyridine (PDB ID: 5VJG; Zn-N of 2.476 A and 2.404 A).

In contrast, the ligands least prone to coordinating with the metal were Phen4 (p-CH3) and Phen18 (p-Br), displaying Zn-N distances of 4.25 +- 0.2 A and 5.19 +- 0.5 A from 100 to 125 ns of MD, respectively, during the same period of significant variations indicated by the RMSD analysis (Fig. 3B), i.e., both compounds remained close to the catalytic residues and the metal until approximately 100 ns. Later, these Zn-N bonds became less persistent. In general, these zinc-ligand interactions could impair the binding of the nucleophilic water molecule and the substrate itself and, consequently, the progress of catalysis.

To assess the impact of residue-fluctuations in each ligand-protein complex, we calculated the difference root-mean-square fluctuation (DeltaRMSF) for all simulations by comparing the six ligand-TcGP63 complexes with the holoenzyme form (Fig. 3C). Our analysis revealed a general loss of mobility (i.e., positive DeltaRMSF values) in the Cys83-Cys100 loop/beta-sheet region (Fig. 3D), with variations >= + 2.5 A, compared to the holoenzyme (Fig. 3C), except for Phen14, which displayed a gain of mobility (i.e., negative DeltaRMSF values) in this same region compared to the holoenzyme. Additionally, the Phe360-Phe511 loop/beta-sheet region (yellow, Fig. 3D) showed a gain in mobility in all cases, but more pronounced for Phen14 and Phen4, compared to the holo-structure (Fig. 3C). Since these two regions are situated more than 7 A away from the active site, these fluctuations should not be directly caused by any close contact with the ligands, except for Phen4 and Phen18, which tend to leave the active site.

When evaluating the Asp279-Trp290 loop (Fig. 3D) close to the active site (surface in gray, Fig. 3D), we observed that, although the DeltaRMSF values remain below l2.5 Al, there is a tendency toward reduced mobility (DeltaRMSF > 0), compared to the holoenzyme (Fig. 3C), except for Phen10 and Phen14, which exhibit increased mobility (DeltaRMSF < 0) in this same region.
Principal component and free energy landscape analysis

To understand the motions and conformational stability of the six ligand-enzyme complexes during the MD simulations, we performed principal component analysis (PCA) considering the protein Calpha atoms (Fig. S3). The first two eigenvectors account for 33.56-67.11% of the total motion in each ligand-protein complex (Fig. S3). Notably, Phen14 (p-F), which shows the most significant increase in mobility in the Phe360-Phe511 region, exhibits the highest movement contribution in PC1 (54.86%). Meanwhile, Phen18 (p-Br) presents similar contributions from PC1 (18.97%) and PC2 (14.59%), possibly associated with the ligand exiting the active site around 130 ns. Such a pattern would be expected for Phen4 (p-CH3); however, because the ligand gradually leaves the binding site, its effect on PC1 is less pronounced.

The free energy landscape (FEL) maps (Figs. S4 and S5) were plotted using the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2), using the InfleCS (inflection core state) program, to determine representative conformations from the MD simulations trajectories, allowing to locate minimum (blue, more stable state) and maximum (red, less stable state) energy conformational spaces.

Analyzing the active site comprising residues Ala174-Leu191 (yellow), Gly204-Ser211 (blue), Glu212-Met238 (red), and Leu277-Thr310 (cyan) that includes catalytic Glu221 and the zinc-binding histidines (220, 224, and 289) (see Fig. S4), we observed that Phen7 (p-OCH3), Phen10 (p-CN), Phen14 (p-F), and Phen17 (p-Cl) remained stable within the active site (Fig. S4). The variations in Calpha atoms occurred mainly in the Ala174-Leu182 (yellow) and Glu280-Leu287 (cyan) loops (Fig. S4).

In contrast, Phen4 (p-CH3) and Phen18 (p-Br) showed two minimum energy clusters: the most populated cluster corresponds to the ligand displaced from the zinc ion (i.e., catalytic site), whereas the least populated cluster represents the initial frames of the MD simulation (Fig. S5).
Hydrogen-bond analysis

Based on the H-bond network patterns observed in all MD simulations (Figs. 4 and S6), we found that Phen7 (p-OCH3), Phen10 (p-CN), Phen14 (p-F), and Phen17 (p-Cl) maintain a binding mode within the enzyme active site very similar to that observed in the poses calculated by molecular docking. However, for these compounds, the H-bonds previously established between the 2-amino group (NH) and Gly284 vanish, probably due to increased flexibility in the Glu280-Leu287 loop, favoring interactions with catalytic Glu221 and zinc-binding His224 (Fig. 4).

It is essential to emphasize that Glu221 is reported to participate in the catalytic activity of zinc-dependent metallopeptidase in conjunction with zinc ion to deprotonate a water molecule, allowing its nucleophilic attack on a peptide bond. Consequently, these interactions explain the average Zn-N(1) distances and highlight the importance of electron-withdrawing groups by inductive effect at the R-substituent for Zn(II) coordination.

The H-bonds between ligands (licorice in cyan) and residues (CPK in cyan) are represented by dashed green lines, such as the metal (in gray) interaction. Regarding Phen4 (p-CH3), we observed that the interaction with Glu221 (30.5%) remains throughout the first 80 ns of the simulation, consistent with the Zn-N(1) distance. However, that interaction with the zinc ion is replaced by a weak interaction with Thr181 (10.1%), keeping the compound in the active site (Fig. S7). As for Phen18 (p-Br), hydrogen bonds with Glu221 vary in a lifetime (27-64.8%), but only during the first 140 ns, after which all interactions are lost in the final 60 ns (Fig. S7). This behavior indicates that this ligand leaves the active site, corroborating the previous analyses.
Binding free energy by linear interaction energy

To obtain the binding free energies (DeltaGbind) between the ligands and TcGP63, the linear interaction energy (LIE) approach was employed, which is comparable to other end-point methods, such as molecular mechanics/Poisson-Boltzmann surface area (MM/PBSA), and both can achieve similar correlation coefficients when compared to experimental data.

The DeltaGbind analysis (Table 2) aligns with the interactions observed in the MD simulations. Phen10 (p-CN) and Phen7 (p-OCH3), featuring R-substituents with electron-withdrawing groups by inductive effect, exhibited the most favorable DeltaGbind values of -9.29 and - 8.88 kcal/mol, respectively. The steric nonpolar interactions (van der Waals), modeled by a Lennard-Jones (LJ) potential, and electrostatic interactions, represented by Coulomb (C) potential, revealed similarity for both ligands (Table 2). Additionally, Phen7 and Phen10 compounds exhibited the best RMSD values (~ 4.0 A) for the complexes and the greatest persistence in the observed hydrogen bonds (~ 92%), confirming their pronouncedly favorable DeltaGbind values (Table 2).

Table 2 also presents the average energy values for steric (LJ) and electrostatic (C) interaction energies for Phen-TcGP63 simulations calculated during the stability period of the ligand-protein complexes. In general, the interaction energy trajectory averages results reveal that the Phen-TcGP63 bound state was lower than those for its free state. The same pattern was observed for steric and electrostatic interactions, indicating that the binding of Phen to TcGP63 was favorable.

passages.text: The compounds with halogenated substituents, Phen14 (p-F) and Phen17 (p-Cl), exhibited no substantial difference due to contributions from van der Waals or electrostatic interaction energies. Their average DeltaGbind values ranged from - 6.82 to -7.53 kcal/mol, respectively. In contrast, compound Phen18 (p-Br), which displayed higher volume between the halogenated substituents, had the lowest energetic contribution to the complex formation, with a DeltaGbind value of -3.29 kcal/mol (Table 2).

Furthermore, electrostatic interaction seems to be a significant factor for ligand binding as it contributes significantly to complex formation, and this compound (Phen18) presented the lowest Coulomb contribution (C-bound = -21.7 kcal/mol) compared to the others (Table 2).

We analyzed the individual contributions of the residues that constitute the active site region (Ala174-Leu191, Gly204-Ser211, Glu212-Met238, and Leu277-Thr310) to ligand interactions (Figs. S8-S12). The primary energetic contributions for Phen4 (p-CH3) came from residues Tyr181 (DeltaGtotal = -3.54 kcal/mol), Trp184 (DeltaGtotal = -6.50 kcal/mol), and Glu283 (DeltaGtotal = -3.99 kcal/mol) (Fig. S8). These residues (Tyr181, Trp184, and Glu283) benefited from van der Waals interactions with the substituted phenyl ring, resulting in LJ contributions of -1.56, -3.64, and - 2.14 kcal/mol, and Coulomb contributions of -1.96, -2.86, and - 1.86 kcal/mol, respectively (Fig. S8).

These interactions of individual residues from the active site region were reflected in the observed binding free energy value presented in Table 2. For Phen7 (p-OCH3), the most significant energetic contribution came from residues Tyr179 (DeltaGtotal = -11.1 kcal/mol) and Ile303 (DeltaGtotal = -7.13 kcal/mol) in van der Waals interaction with the 1,10-phenanthroline ring favored by an LJ value of -5.66 and - 3.89 kcal/mol, respectively (Fig. S9). These contributions resulted in a conformation that allowed the persistence of the observed binding with Glu221, as previously mentioned.

The leading energetic contributions to the binding of Phen10 (p-CN) came from Tyr181, which interacts with the 1,10-phenanthroline ring, yielding DeltaGtotal of -1.38 kcal/mol. Additional contributions were observed from residues Glu283 (DeltaGtotal = -2.27 kcal/mol), Gly284 (DeltaGtotal = -1.76 kcal/mol), and Ala286 (DeltaGtotal = -3.26 kcal/mol), which interact with the substituted phenyl ring (Fig. S10). These residues facilitate the necessary conformation to form hydrogen bonds with Glu221 and Tyr186. Moreover, a significant Lennard-Jones contribution of -2.64 kcal/mol was noted with catalytic His224, which helps stabilize the ligand within the active site. Furthermore, this ligand (Phen10) demonstrated the most significant number of residues (80 in total) that had energetic contributions reinforcing its binding to the target (Fig. S10), highlighting its high binding free energy value in comparison to the five other ligands (see Table 2).

Similarly, Phen14 (p-F) and Phen17 (p-Cl) showed contributions consistent with previously discussed. The most significant residues were Trp184, Tyr186, His224, and Gly284. The Lennard-Jones values ranged from - 1.37 to -4.06 kcal/mol, while the Coulomb values fell between - 1.18 and - 4.69 kcal/mol (Figs. S11 and S12). This resulted in a DeltaGtotal ranging from - 3.89 to -8.75 kcal/mol (Figs. S11 and S12). To these compounds (Phen14 and Phen17), we observed that the imidazole ring of histidine is positioned towards the phenyl rings of the ligand, potentially establishing some favorable hydrophobic interactions for the binding mode. As expected, Phen18 had the lowest number of residues contributing to energy, with only five residues identified, namely Arg178, Tyr181, Trp184, and Tyr285. The Lennard-Jones energy values for these residues ranged from - 0.52 to -4.91 kcal/mol, while the Coulomb energy values varied from - 0.58 to -5.09 kcal/mol. This resulted in DeltaGtotal ranging from - 1.13 to -10 kcal/mol (Fig. S13).

The N-phenyl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines demonstrate promise as a viable class of compounds targeting the Trypanosoma cruzi GP63 metalloenzyme. Electron-withdrawing groups by inductive effect as R-phenyl substituents, facilitate the formation of persistent hydrogen bonds between the 2-amino group of these compounds and the carboxylate group of the catalytic Glu221 residue, according to our MD simulations, thereby enhancing the binding mode of these compounds. This interaction allows proximity to the catalytic residues and the metal cofactor. Furthermore, halogenated substituents contribute significantly to the active pocket's binding mode.
Materials and methods
Protein comparative modeling and ligands preparation

The 3D structural model of TcGP63 (i.e., Trypanosoma cruzi leishmanolysin-like peptidase) was built by comparative modeling, following a previously published workflow, using the SWISS-MODEL server (https://swissmodel.expasy.org/interactive). The T. cruzi GP63 target amino acid residue sequence in the FASTA format was obtained from the UniProtKB database (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/), under the accession code Q9NG31 (leishmanolysin-like peptidase, EC: 3.4.24.36). The template 3D structure was the Leishmania major GP63 (leishmanolysin or major surface glycoprotein, EC: 3.4.24.36) enzyme (PDB: 1LML, resolution: 1.86 A) obtained from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) (https://www.rcsb.org/).

This TcGP63 model is available in the ModelArchive repository at https://www.modelarchive.org/doi/10.5452/ma-2ks25 (deposition is password protected, waiting for publication). The sequence alignments were performed at the T-Coffee server (http://tcoffee.crg.cat/) using structural alignments (Expresso) T-Coffee. The identity (30.71%) and similarity (43.57%) of each sequence pair were evaluated using the Sequence Manipulation Suite server (https://www.bioinformatics.org/sms2/ident_sim.html).

The 2D and 3D structures of each compound were sketched and constructed in the Marvin Sketch software (https://chemaxon.com/marvin), and geometry optimization was performed using the MMFF94 force field in the same software (ChemAxon, https://chemaxon.com/products/marvin).
Molecular docking simulations

The molecular docking simulations were performed using the GOLD (v. 2022.3) (Genetic Optimization for Ligand Docking) program, applying the four available score functions, namely the Astex statistical potential (ASP), piecewise linear potential (ChemPLP), GoldScore, and ChemScore, according to the protocol and parameters previously described by our research group. The Phen-TcGP63 complexes were centered at the Zn(II) atom (index 6923) included in the 1.93960 x 4.38660 x 1.69410 nm3 box dimensions with a 10 A radius. The final compound classification was made by the scale method according to Eq. (1):
In Eq. (1), w/W = ASP fitness score; x/X = ChemPLP fitness score; y/Y = ChemScore; z/Z = GoldScore; Min = lowest fitness score value; Max = highest fitness score value.

The validation and choice of the pose for interactions analysis was made by consensus, considering the lowest RMSD (<= 2.00 A) among the four score functions. The interaction of the ligands with TcGP63 was analyzed with the BIOVIA Discovery Studio Visualizer (v. 2021) program, and the figures of the binding poses were constructed with PyMOL (v. 3.5).
Molecular dynamics simulations

The molecular dynamics simulations were performed using the GROMACS (v. 5.1.4 and 2019) package, applying the CHARMM36 all-atom (AA) force field and TIP3P water model, using as input structures the ligand-protein complexes from the molecular docking results. Before preparing the ligands topologies, the @<TRIPOS> BOND section in the "mol2" file was fixed using the "sort_mol2_bonds.pl" Python script to ensure the ascending order of the atom numbers. Then, each ligand topology was acquired through the CHARMM general force field program for organic molecules (CGenFF) via the CGenFF server (https://cgenff.umaryland.edu/initguess/).

The ionization states of the protein's residues were adjusted to pH 7.4 using the "pdb2gmx" Python script. Each complex was centered inside a cubic periodic box (51.84 A x 43.72 A x 41.26 A, volume: 935.1 A3), solvated with water TIP3P type, and neutralized with five Na+ cations. Systems were submitted to energy minimization steps, according to our previous protocol, using a convergence criterion of 1000 kJ.mol-1. nm-1 followed by gradient conjugate until 100 kJ.mol-1.nm-1. The minimized systems were submitted to two consecutive equilibration steps, considering 300 K of temperature and 1 bar of pressure, during 1 ns and position restraint for both ligand and enzyme. First, volume and temperature are considered constant, and then the system is considered isothermal-isobaric.

Hydrogen atoms in the system were frozen using the LINCS algorithm, the long-range electrostatic interactions were treated using the PME (particle mesh Ewald) algorithm, and a cut-off radius of 10 A was applied to both electrostatic and steric (van der Waals) interactions. After the thermalization step, the molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed during 200 ns, using 2 fs integration time and 20 A of cut-off radius to the long-range interactions (i.e., electrostatic).

The Phen-TcGP63 complexes in aqueous systems were evaluated by the root mean square deviations (RMSD) and root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) calculations during the MD simulation time. In the RMSD analysis, the protein versus ligand interaction was evaluated considering the centers of mass of the protein Calpha atoms and the ligand. In contrast, in the RMSF analysis, the flexibility of individual protein residues was evaluated considering the protein Calpha atoms. The hydrogen bonding (H-bond) intermolecular interactions were computed assuming a cut-off distance between donor (D) and acceptor (A) atoms of 4.0 A and a cut-off H-D-A angle of 30  by the GROMACS 2019 package. The H-bonds frequency was calculated using the "hbmap2grace" package. Figures were constructed using the Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD) program (http://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/vmd/).
Principal component and free energy landscape analysis

Principal component analysis (PCA) was employed to investigate the conformational dynamics of TcGP63 by considering the Calpha coordinates. We use the MDAnalysis library with the "PCAauto" script, available in a public repository. Each trajectory frame was aligned to the first frame, and a 3 Nx3 N covariance matrix was built, where N is the number of Calpha atoms. Diagonalization of this matrix yielded eigenvectors (principal components, PCs) ordered by their associated eigenvalues, representing the variance in motion.

The first two principal components (PC1 and PC2), catching most of the variance in the data, were selected for free energy landscape (FEL) analysis using the inference of connectivity of states (InfleCS) method. The FEL was built along the PCs of the clustering object, considering the number of PCs ranged from two to ten, with five iterations, 80 grids, and a temperature of 300 K. The density and the FEL were estimated by using Gaussian mixture models. Cluster centers were determined by the coordinates used to extract trajectory frames corresponding to an energy minimum cluster center in the PCs. FEL analysis was performed with the "InfleCS-analysis" script, accessible in a public repository.
Binding free energy estimation by the linear interaction energy method

The binding free energy (DeltaGbind) was calculated using the linear interaction energy (LIE) method with standard coefficients alpha = 0.161 and beta = 0.50 through the module added to the GROMACS (v. 5.1.4.) considering the 200 ns of the MD simulations.
Conclusions

The present study has focused on how a series of N-aryl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines (Phen1-Phen20), containing a nitrogen-heterocycle nucleus known as metal-chelating and showing in vitro anti-trypanosomal activity, could interact with our comparative 3D model of the Trypanosoma cruzi GP63 (TcGP63) zinc-metalloenzyme, since there is currently no experimental structure available, through an in silico approach by molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.

The consensus docking of these 20 compounds in the enzyme active site with the four GOLD scoring functions (GoldScore, ChemPLP, ChemScore, and ASP) revealed that N-(R-phenyl) derivatives (R = methyl, methoxy, trifluoromethyl, cyanide, nitro, fluorine, chlorine, and bromine), had better fitness scores than the N-naphthyl ones, with the para-substituted compounds, namely Phen4 (p-CH3), Phen7 (p-OCH3), Phen10 (p-CN), Phen14 (p-F), Phen17 (p-Cl), and Phen18 (p-Br), being more favorable than ortho or meta ones. Among these top six compounds, Phen7 and Phen10 scored the highest. Still, all six revealed the same docking pose in the TcGP63 active site, presenting at least three interactions in common, one between phenanthroline N-atoms and Zn(II)-cofactor; an H-bond between 2-amino group and Gly284 and a pi-stacking between N-phenyl and imidazole of zinc-binding His224.

Subsequent MD simulation with GROMACS package and CHARMM36 force field of aqueous (TIP3P) ligand-protein complexes for these six standout compounds revealed that Phen7, Phen10, Phen14, and Phen17 remain within the active site throughout the entire simulation time (200 ns). At the same time, Phen4 leaves gradually and Phen18 leaves suddenly after 130 ns, consistent with the measurements of the average ligand-metal (N-Zn) distance, shorter (2.18-2.57 A) for the first four, and longer (4.25-5.19 A) for the last two in the final half of the simulation. Phen7, Phen10, Phen14, and Phen17 maintain a binding mode within the active site, like the docking poses, showing the same N-Zn(II) interaction. Still, the H-bonding involving the 2-amino group now occurs with catalytic Glu221 and zinc-binding His224 rather than Gly284, probably due to the greater flexibility of loop Glu280-Leu287. Notably, Phen7 and Phen10 exhibited the most favorable and stable interactions during MD simulations, with lower RMSD values and more remarkable H-bond persistence. A binding free energy calculation by the linear interaction energy (LIE) method supported these findings, highlighting Phen7 and Phen10 as the most promising candidates, with DeltaGbind values of -8.53 and - 8.22 kcal/mol, respectively, which were also the top two ranked compounds by consensus docking.

These findings suggest that electron-withdrawing groups by inductive effect as R-substituents, such as p-OCH3 (Phen7) and p-CN (Phen10), are crucial for enhancing the binding mode of N-phenyl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines to the TcGP63 model, bringing them closer to Zn(II)-cofactor, catalytic Glu221, and zinc-binding His224. These results emphasize the potential of N-phenyl-1,10-phenanthroline-2-amines as effective inhibitors of the T. cruzi GP63 enzyme, which could lead to the development of new trypanocidal agents in the fight against Chagas disease. This neglected disease is targeted for elimination by 2030 as part of the global Sustainable Development Goals.

passages.text: Comprehensive analysis of the effects of cooking conditions on the quality, sensory characteristics, and flavor profile of glutinous rice chicken, a Chinese traditional poultry meat product

This study investigated the effects of cooking conditions on cooking loss, texture, and sensory attributes of glutinous rice chicken (GRC), a popular Chinese poultry dish. We compared the nutritional and sensory profiles of GRC prepared under optimal conditions (GRC-OP) with those of a commercial product (CG). Cooking time, power, and pressure significantly affected the shear force, hardness, and sensory qualities of GRC. The optimal parameters were determined using an orthogonal design: 20 min cooking time, 1000 watts power, and 60 kPa pressure. Gas chromatography/mass spectrometry and E-nose analyses showed that GRC-OP had a volatile profile similar to that of CG but with higher levels of specific compounds, including heptanal, 2-heptenal, octanal, hexanol, octanol, and 1-nonen-4-ol. GRC-OP also exhibited superior umami, salty, and rich tastes, and higher amino acid content, particularly Asp, Glu, Thr, Ser, Ala, Val, Met, and Ile. These findings provide crucial data for optimizing the quality and nutritional value of GRC in the meat industry.
Highlights
Identify the optimal processing parameters for glutinous rice chicken.
Keep the characteristics of the Yanbian Korean nationality glutinous rice chicken.
Eating quality and flavor properties of GRC-OP were superior to CG.
The content of free amino acids of GRC-OP were superior to CG.
Introduction

Poultry meat and products are rich in nutrients such as proteins, minerals, and vitamins, which are an indispensable part of the daily diet. According to previous studies, the cholesterol and saturated fatty acid contents in poultry meat are lower than those in red meat because of its low price, high nutritional value, and favorable sensory characteristics. Poultry meat and poultry products have attracted increasing attention from consumers. Glutinous rice chicken (GRC), a traditional meat product of the Yanbian Korean nationality, is highly regarded by consumers owing to its palatable taste and distinctive qualities. GRC is a Korean diet made by steaming and cooking rural free-range chicken and glutinous rice as the main processing materials and adding ingredients such as nourishing ginseng, red dates, and wolfberries. In addition to the oily aroma of chicken, diners can perceive the soft, waxy, and refreshing tastes of the other ingredients. Consequently, GRC can fulfill the gustatory needs of consumers and provide nutritional supplementation, representing a highly representative dietary option within traditional Korean culinary traditions. Most GRC products are produced through a traditional process that lacks standardization of processing technology. This often results in uneven quality of the final product with a high degree of yield instability, which in turn leads to a significant amount of waste in the production process.

The traditional manufacturing steps of GRC include steaming and cooking with rural free-range chicken and glutinous rice as the main processing materials, and adding ingredients such as nourishing ginseng, red dates, and wolfberries. The quality of cooked meat, particularly its flavor, is significantly affected by factors such as temperature and heating time. The cooking temperature and time are crucial factors in product processing because they significantly affect protein oxidation and denaturation. It is important to note that these factors should be carefully controlled to ensure optimal product quality. Subjecting chicken protein hydrolysate to temperatures above 60  C for 20 min results in complete elimination of the >10,000 Da fraction, indicating extensive protein degradation. Similarly, in beef broth, free amino acids decrease at temperatures above 75  C and cooking times exceeding 120 min. Furthermore, longer cooking times lead to increased levels of glutamic acid, aspartic acid, lysine, and methionine, all of which are strongly associated with flavor. Thus, heat treatment affects protein degradation and hydrolysis, which significantly alters the flavor of meat products during processing. evaluated the taste profile of traditional Chinese Fuliji red-cooked chicken (FRCC) in different processing steps, including raw, frying, stewing, vacuum packaging, and sterilization, by measuring sodium chloride (NaCl), sugar, free amino acids (FAAs), nucleotides, and flavor. used the headspace gas chromatography-ion mobility spectrometry (HS-GC-IMS) technique to identify the main volatile substances formed during the processing of Dezhou braised chicken (DBC). also investigated the effects of cooking temperature (75, 80, 85, 90, 95, and 100  C) and cooking time (10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 90, and 120 min) on protein degradation, protein oxidation, and flavor formation in stewed chicken meat. Although many studies have been conducted on the quality characteristics and processing technologies of chicken products, both domestically and internationally, few have focused on optimizing the processing technology and quality of traditional Chinese GRC.

In this study, traditional processing technology for GRC was employed in conjunction with a pressure cooker. By controlling the cooking time, cooking temperature, and cooking pressure during the cooking process, a single-factor test was performed to investigate the influence of cooking conditions on the physicochemical properties and sensory evaluation of GRC, and an orthogonal test was conducted to obtain the optimal conditions. In addition, the aroma compounds of GRC were investigated and compared using HS-SPME-GC/MS, electronic nose, and electronic tongue methods. Based on the results, theoretical guidance can be provided for the realization of standardized, large-scale, and industrialized production of GRC products.
Materials and methods
Sample preparation
Simplified schematic diagram of the preparation of glutinous rice chicken.
Fig. 1

A simplified schematic of the study is shown in Fig. 1. Native chickens at 42 days of age and purchased from Yanji West Market (Yanji, Jilin, China) were used in this study. Briefly, qualified slaughtered native chickens were selected and dehaired, and the internal organs, bursa of Fabricius (chicken tip), and fat blocks were removed, followed by cleaning with distilled water. Subsequently, 2500-3000 mL of distilled water was poured into a pressure cooker, after which clean native chicken (approximately 2000 g-2500 g) was added. Additionally, 30 g of scallion, 20 g of onion, 10 g of ginger, 10 g of garlic, and 1 g of astragalus root were added to the pressure cooker, and cooked in an induction cooker at high heat (power 1600 W-2100 W) until boiling, and then cooled to low heat (500-1400 W). Glutinous rice was purchased from the Yanji West Market (Yanji, Jilin, China). The glutinous rice was washed and soaked in cold water for 3 h. Subsequently, the following ingredients were added to the pot: 850 g of glutinous rice, 30 g of red dates, 1 g of astragalus, 1 g of walnuts, 15 g of raisins, 7 g of dried cranberries, and 2 g of dried blueberries. Subsequently, 1300 g of chicken stock and steam were added for 35 min. Subsequently, the glutinous rice was stirred thoroughly. The final step in preparing the GRC was to place the cooked chicken on top of the glutinous rice. Chicken meat was bonded, ground, and sampled at a chicken-to-rice weight (7:4). Partial freezing of samples from the GRC to -80  C was performed for the determination of nutrient content, E-nose, E-tongue, FAAS, and volatile flavor compounds. The remaining samples were used for texture profile analysis (TPA) and cooking loss measurements.
Single-factor and orthogonal experiments

A one-factor test program was developed based on cooking time, power, and pressure: (a) The cooking power was set at 1000 W (140  C) and the cooking pressure was set at 70 kPa, and the effects on sensory quality, cooking loss, shear force, and texture of GRC were investigated when the cooking time was 15 min, 20 min, 25 min, 30 min, and 35 min. (b) The cooking time was set to 25 min and the cooking pressure was 70 kPa, and the effects on sensory quality, cooking loss, shear force, and texture of GRC were investigated when the cooking power was 500 W (100  C), 800 W (120  C), 1000 W (140  C), 1200 W (160  C), and 1400 W (180  C). (c) The cooking time was set to 25 min and the cooking power was set to 1000 W (140  C), and the effects on sensory quality, cooking loss, shear force, and texture of GRC were investigated when the cooking pressure was 50 kPa, 60 kPa, 70 kPa, 80 kPa, and 90 kPa. Table S1 lists the orthogonal test factors and their corresponding levels. Based on the results of the one-way test, three factors-cooking time (A), cooking power (B), and cooking pressure (C)-were selected for the L9 (33) orthogonal test using the sensory composite score as the criterion.
Sensory evaluation

Sensory evaluation was performed by 10 trained and experienced professionals (five males and five females, aged 20-30 years) from the Food Research Centre of Yanbian University. The appearance, color, texture, smell, taste, and overall acceptability of the dishes were evaluated according to the Chinese national standards (QB/T 5471-2020). The scores for each aspect range from 1 to 20, with 20 being the best and 1 being the worst. The highest score for the sensory evaluation of the GRC products was 100. The sensory scoring standards are listed in Table S2.

Individuals participating in the sensory experiment were informed of the protocol and volunteered to participate. Before this study, the sensory analysis was approved by the College of Agriculture, Yanbian University, and all participants provided informed consent. All participants' rights and privacy were well protected, and consent was obtained for the collection and use of their personal information and related experimental data.
TPA

The TPA of each sample was measured using a texture analyzer (TMS-PLUS, FT, US) equipped with a 12.7 mm flat cylindrical probe. The samples were cut into cubes (1 x 1 x 1 cm) along the direction of the muscle fibers. The test speed was set to 4.0 mm/s, and the post-test speed was the default test speed in TPA mode. The trigger force was 0.07 N, and two consecutive cycles of 40 % compression were performed with 6 s between cycles. Shear force, hardness, springiness, cohesiveness, gumminess, and chewiness were recorded.
Cooking loss

The cooked samples were drained of excess liquid using a plastic net and weighed individually. Cooking loss was calculated as the weight difference between the uncooked and cooked samples and expressed as g/100 g. The average cooking loss value (n = 3) was then calculated and presented as the mean +- standard error.
Moisture, protein, fat, and sodium chloride contents

The moisture, protein, and sodium chloride contents of the GRC were measured according to the national standards GB5009.3-2016, GB5009.44-2016, and GB5009.5-2016, respectively. The fat content was determined according to the method described by with the following modifications. Chicken meat (2 g) was added to 25 mL of trichloromethane-methanol solution (2:1, v/v) and homogenized for 1 min, after which 15 mL of trichloromethane-methanol solution was added, mixed well, and allowed to stand for 1 h before filtration. To the obtained filtrate, 8.8 mL of a mixed solution containing 7.3 g/L NaCl and 0.5 g/L CaCl2 was added. The mixture was then centrifuged at 3000g for 15 min. The liquid at the top was discarded. The remaining liquid fraction was evaporated using a rotary evaporator and dried to a constant weight under a vacuum. The fat content was determined as the difference in weight between the flasks before and after spin distillation.
Volatile flavor compound analysis

The volatile flavor compounds in GRC were determined using solid-phase microextraction (SPME). This method was based on that described by, with minor modifications. Volatile compounds were extracted from the headspace (HS) of the bacon samples by using SPME fiber (Shimadzu Corporation, Kyoto, Japan) coated with a 75 mum layer (Supelco, Bellefonte, PA, USA) of (DVB/CAR/PDMS). Two grams of the sample were transferred to a dedicated headspace vial, and the gas was equilibrated at 25  C room temperature for 15 min. The sample was then extracted using a 75 mum PDMS/DVB fiber tip in a sand bath at 60  C for 30 min.

Gas-phase conditions: Volatile substances were separated using a capillary column DB-5MS 30 m 0.25 mm, film thickness of 0.25 mum (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). The SPME fiber was desorbed and maintained in the injection port at 280  C during the whole chromatographic run. The carrier gas was helium at 18.5 psi, resulting in a flow of 1 mL/min at 40  C. The oven temperature was held at 40  C for 3 min, increased from 40  C to 120  C at 5  C/min, held at 120  C for 5 min, and then increased from 120  C to 230  C at 10  C/min with a final hold time of 5 min. Mass spectrometry conditions: MS operated in electron impact mode at an electron impact energy of 70 eV and 200  C with an interface temperature of 280  C and a collected data rate of 1 scan s-1 over a range of m/z 30-550. Compounds were characterized by searching the NIST08 and NIST08s spectral libraries, and for compounds with a qualitative match of >80, the relative content was calculated using the normalization method.
Electronic nose (E-nose) analysis

E-nose analysis (PEN3; Airsense, Germany) of the GRC was performed as described by with slight modifications. Briefly, approximately 5 g of meat was placed in a 20 mL clean E-nose injection vial, sealed, and gas-equilibrated for 15 min. The E-nose detection experiments were conducted with the following parameters: flush time, 120 s; sample preparation time, 5 s; detection time, 60 s; internal flow rate, 200 mL/min; and inlet flow rate, 200 mL/min. The E-nose contains 10 single-thick-film metal oxide sensors: W1C, W5S, W3C, W6S, W5C,W1S, W1W, W2S, W2W, and W3S. The results are reported as the average of three replicates.
Electronic tongue (E-tongue) analysis

The taste properties of GRC were determined using an E-tongue system (SA-402B; Insent, Tokyo, Japan). The method described by was used with slight modifications. About 9 g of meat sample was added to 90 mL of distilled, followed by homogenization and centrifugation at 4  C, 10000g for 10 min. The supernatants were obtained from the samples and filtered. A sample measurement program (two-step wash) was used to determine the five tastes: umami, salty, sour, bitter, and astringent. Each group was replicated three times and each replicate was measured four times in parallel.
FAAs

The sample (3 g) was weighed, 30 mL of deionized water was added, homogenized in an ice bath for 1 min, and centrifuged at 10000g for 30 min at 4  C. The supernatant was filtered. Ten milliliters of the filtrate were added to 20 mL of 4 % TCA and incubated at 37  C for 30 min. The supernatant was collected and assayed on a 0.45 mum organic filter membrane. The whole process was performed at 0-4  C. FAA were determined using an automated amino acid analyzer (L-8800, Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan).
Data analysis

The test data were categorized using Excel, and a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS 27 for GRC volatile flavors. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. At least three independent replicates were performed for each experiment, and the results were expressed as mean +- standard deviation (SD).

The effect of cooking time on the sensory properties of GRC is shown in Fig. 2A. As the cooking time increased, the sensory scores of GRC increased significantly at the beginning of 25 min and then decreased for cooking times longer than 25 min. At 15, 20, and 25 min, GRC had a delicate taste and better appearance than the others. When the cooking time was more than 25 min, the structure of the GRC began to loosen, and the meat became rotten, with deterioration of the texture. An insufficient cooking time prevents chicken proteins from being fully denatured, resulting in poor quality. However, overcooking negatively affects the tissue structure and flavor. Extended cooking times and high-temperature cooking can lead to the denaturation and decomposition of chicken proteins, respectively, which can negatively affect the quality of the final products. Table 1A shows the cooking loss and TPA of the GRC at different cooking times. The cooking loss of chicken meat gradually increased, reaching a maximum of 23.46 % at 30 min, and then decreased slightly to 23.16 % at 35 min. Similar findings were reported by, who found that a longer cooking time may contribute to higher cooking loss. Moreover, the shear force and hardness exhibited an overall increasing trend and then decreased after 30 min. There were no significant changes in springiness, cohesiveness, gumminess, or chewiness (p < 0.5). Based on sensory evaluation, the optimal cooking time for GRC was estimated to be between 15 and 25 min. Therefore, cooking times of 15, 20, and 25 min were selected for optimization in this study.
Effect of cooking power on cooking loss, TPA, and sensory quality of GRC

Fig. 2B shows the effect of cooking power on the sensory evaluation of GRC. As the cooking power increased from 800 to 1000 W, the GRC sensory scores exhibited a slight decline from 800 W to 1000 W. However, they generally demonstrated an upward trend, reaching a maximum value of 76.63 at 1200 W. GRC cooked at 500 W of cooking power had a lower sensory score, probably because of the lower temperature in the center of the chicken, which made it less palatable. The results showed that the sensory quality of chicken increased with a corresponding increase in cooking power, and the overall sensory quality score showed an increasing and then a decreasing trend. Table 1B shows the cooking loss and TPA of GRC at different cooking power levels. The cooking loss appeared to remain relatively stable when the cooking power was between 500 and 1000 W. However, it increased significantly above 1000 W, reaching a maximum of 23.28 % at 1400 W. There was no significant difference in cooking loss when the cooking power was 1200 W and 1400 W. The rate of cooking loss is a crucial indicator of the muscle water-holding capacity (WHC). When proteins are in a tight state, they have a limited capacity for network space, which results in low WHC. Conversely, when proteins in the expanded state have a large network space, this results in an enhanced WHC. In the current study, moisture loss occurred in GRC samples as a result of heated cooking, which agrees with the results of, who indicated that during cooking, myosin and actin denatured and expelled the sarcoplasmic fluids from the muscle fibers, together with shrinkage of the perimysium, resulting in water loss from the meat tissue. Moreover, the shear force tends to increase, and the shear force of 1000 W-1400 W is significantly higher than that of 500 W and 800 W. And the hardness value of chicken meat first decreased and then increased with increasing cooking power, followed by a slight decrease at 1200 W. However, gumminess tended to decrease and then increase to a maximum at 1000 W, and there were no significant differences in springiness, cohesiveness, shear, and chewiness. In conclusion, the optimum cooking power was selected for orthogonal experiments at three levels: 800, 1000, and 1200 W.
Effect of cooking pressure on cooking loss, TPA, and sensory quality of GRC

The effects of cooking pressure on the sensory evaluation of GRC are shown in Fig. 2C. With increasing cooking pressure, the sensory scores of GRC gradually increased and then decreased, reaching a maximum value of 81.63 at 60 kPa. Although it was difficult to eliminate the fishy taste of chicken, a higher cooking pressure could change the spatial structure between myogenic fibers and reduce texture and chewiness. The decomposition of chicken flavor and aroma substances is accelerated under high cooking pressure, which adversely affects the chicken flavor. Table 1C shows the cooking loss and TPA of GRC under different cooking pressures. There was no significant difference in cooking loss at cooking pressures of 50 kPa-70 kPa. The shear force of chicken meat first decreased and then increased, and the trends in hardness, springiness, and chewiness were consistent with those of the shear force, all of which initially decreased and then increased. Cohesiveness and gumminess gradually decreased at 50 kPa-70 kPa, increased, and slightly decreased at 90 kPa. In conclusion, 60, 70, and 80 kPa were selected as the optimal small-fire cooking pressures for orthogonal experiments.
Analysis of orthogonal experiment results

Based on the single-factor results, an orthogonal test was performed to determine the optimal cooking conditions for GRC (Table S3). The results of the polarity analysis showed that RA > RB > RC, and the order of influence of the three factors on the sensory evaluation of GRC was as follows: cooking time (A) > cooking power (B) > cooking pressure (C). According to the results of the orthogonal test analysis, the optimal processing conditions for the GRC were A2B2C1.
